title: US Expands Social Media Screening to Journalists, TN and TD Visa Applicants
excerpt: Starting October 1, the State Department adds I, TN, and TD visa applicants to its online-presence review — the latest wave of social media vetting that already covers students, H-1B workers, and more.
body:
• From October 1, 2026, applicants for I (foreign media), TN (USMCA professionals), and TD (their dependents) visas must set all social media profiles to "public" or "open" so consular officers can review them, under a State Department announcement made September 18.
  • This is an expansion, not a new regime: F-1/M-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, and H-1B/H-4 workers were already subject to online-presence review, along with A-3, C-3, G-5, H-3, K, Q, R, S, T and U categories added in March 2026.
  • The State Department says it uses all available information to determine visa eligibility and inadmissibility, including national security and public-safety concerns; no published list of disqualifying content exists.
  • The practical effect for Indian applicants is narrow — I visas for journalists are the main exposure — but consular officers may examine posts, photos, comments, and affiliations across platforms including Facebook, Instagram, X, YouTube, TikTok, and LinkedIn.

The United States will widen its social media screening of visa applicants from today, October 1, 2026, pulling foreign journalists, Canadian and Mexican professionals, and their families into a digital vetting system that has been expanding for more than a year. Under a September 18 announcement from the State Department, applicants for I, TN, and TD nonimmigrant visas will be instructed to set their social media profiles to "public" or "open" to facilitate consular review.

The I visa covers representatives of foreign media working temporarily in the US; the TN visa covers qualifying Canadian and Mexican professionals under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement; the TD visa covers their dependents. Officers may examine posts, photos, comments, and affiliations across platforms including Facebook, Instagram, X, YouTube, TikTok, and LinkedIn as part of visa adjudication.

Context & Background

Mandatory online-presence review has been rolling out in waves. It began with F, M, and J student and exchange visas in June 2025, was extended to H-1B and H-4 workers in December 2025, and broadened in March 2026 to cover A-3, C-3, G-5, H-3, K, Q, R, S, T, and U categories. The October 1 expansion is the latest step in a steady widening of what consular officers examine before approving a visa stamp.

The State Department's rationale has been consistent: "The Department relies on every available source of information during visa screening and vetting to identify applicants who may be inadmissible to the United States, including those who pose a threat to national security or public safety. We apply this rigorous vetting standard consistently across all visa applicants." The agency describes online information as one element of its broader security and eligibility screening process — assessing both whether the applicant qualifies for the requested visa and whether any grounds of inadmissibility apply.

The US first began requiring most visa applicants to submit social media handles on application forms in 2019. Requiring profiles to be public rather than merely listed on the form marks a more aggressive phase: officers can now directly review the content itself rather than relying on whatever is incidentally visible.

Impact & Analysis

For most Indians, this expansion changes little on its own — H-1B, H-4, F-1, F-2, J-1, and J-2 applicants were already under online-presence review, and TN/TD visas are by definition limited to Canadian and Mexican nationals. The group directly caught by the new rule is Indian journalists and media professionals applying for I visas, who must now open their profiles for consular inspection.

What the expansion signals matters more than its immediate reach: student visas, then work visas, then humanitarian and religious categories, now media and USMCA professionals. University international-student offices are telling applicants to treat their online presence as part of the application. Posts inconsistent with an application, or raising security or public-safety flags, can trigger delays or denial, even though the State Department has published no list of disqualifying content.

There is also a practical wrinkle for visa stamping abroad: the announcement governs visa applications at US embassies and consulates, so applicants should address privacy settings and profile content before interviews, not during them.

Diaspora Angle

Indian media professionals assigned to US bureaus — and Indian journalists traveling on temporary assignment — are the clearest Indian exposure to the new rule. More broadly, the steady expansion of digital vetting is another reason Indian families with children in the US on student visas, or professionals on H-1B, are scrubbing timelines and tightening associations long before any interview is scheduled.

What's Next

October 1 also starts FY 2027, resetting the annual green-card number — so applicants enter a fresh visa year under tighter digital scrutiny. Further waves cannot be ruled out; each prior announcement added categories to an existing framework rather than announcing new policy. The practical advice is unchanged: assume officers are reading, set profiles public before the interview, and keep online activity consistent with the application.
nri_angle: Indian journalists on I visas are the main Indian group newly affected; the expansion is another step in digital vetting that already covers the student and H-1B visas most Indians use.
